source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Explicitly built on Newell and Simon: problem solving as search through a tree. Letting the model propose, score and prune partial thoughts beat plain chain of thought on Game of 24.
numbers: Game of 24 (GPT-4): IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC 9.0%, ToT breadth 1 = 45%, breadth 5 = 74%. Oracle best-of-100 CoT = 49%.
quote: problem solving as search through a combinatorial problem space, represented as a tree
limits: Tasks are well-structured with a checkable end state. Search cost is many model calls per item. Not a design task.
agent_relevance: Direct support for S6 search: a tree with a state value and pruning beats more samples on the same node budget. Compare at equal tokens (G7).

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts, Mini Crosswords and Creative Writing results
finding: On a harder 5x5 crossword, search ablations show pruning and backtracking carry most of the gain. In creative writing, ToT raised coherence scores.
numbers: Crosswords (Table 3): ToT letter-level about 78%, word-level about 60%, 4 of 20 games solved; ablations without pruning 65.4/41.5 and without backtracking 54.6/20 (letter/word, read from extracted table text). Creative writing coherency: IO 6.19, CoT 6.93, ToT 7.56; with refine IO 7.67, ToT 7.91.
limits: Table text came from PDF extraction, so column alignment is partly inferred. Creative writing score is a GPT-4 judge, which G5 warns against.
agent_relevance: Backtracking and pruning are the active parts of search. An ill-structured task needs a value function that code can check, not only a model score.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts, cost comparison to sampling
finding: ToT trades compute for success. The paper maps ToT and best-of-k sampling onto nodes visited and finds ToT with breadth above 1 wins at equal node count.
numbers: Best of 100 CoT = 49% vs ToT b=5 = 74% on Game of 24. Thought generation can be i.i.d. sampling, sequential proposing or refining; evaluation by value scoring or by voting.
limits: Only GPT-4 tested. Node-count equivalence is the authors' framing, not equal tokens.
agent_relevance: The value check should run on early partial states before more steps are spent.

source: Zhou et al. (2023/2024) Language Agent Tree Search (LATS)
finding: Monte Carlo tree search over an LLM agent, with environment feedback and self-reflection as value. Reports state-of-the-art code results and competitive web navigation without training.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 92.7% with GPT-4; WebShop average score 75.9 with GPT-3.5 (gradient-free).
quote: they fail to consider multiple reasoning paths or to plan ahead
limits: Needs an environment signal such as unit tests. HumanEval is well-structured. Cost is high.
agent_relevance: Search plus real feedback (G2) is the pattern that works. Fits S6 when a check exists.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) LLMs Can't Plan, But Can Help Planning in LLM-Modulo Frameworks
finding: Autoregressive LLMs alone plan poorly and verify poorly. Pairing the LLM as candidate generator with external verifiers (critique back-prompts) lifts planning a lot where a verifier exists.
numbers: LLM-Modulo: Blocksworld 82% within 15 back-prompting rounds, Logistics 70%, obfuscated Mystery Blocksworld only about 10%.
quote: LLMs Can't Plan, But Can Help Planning
limits: Position paper citing earlier results (Valmeekam et al.). Planning domains are well-structured with formal verifiers. Gain collapses when the model cannot generate plausible candidates.
agent_relevance: Matches 'program decides, model fills a slot'. For ill-structured design there is no formal verifier, so the open question is which code-checkable critics to use.

source: Guo et al. (2025) Toward Engineering AGI: EngDesign benchmark (NeurIPS D&B)
finding: Open-ended engineering design tasks across nine domains, scored by running simulations. Single-shot success is low and most models cannot meet the constraints.
numbers: Best model o3 = 34.38% pass rate (3 trials per task); GPT-4o and Gemini-2.0-Flash about 15%. Analog IC design: 0% for every model. Robustness: o1 0.62, o3 0.61, o4-mini-high 0.57; Gemini-2.0-Flash 0.20, DeepSeek-v3 0.35. Claude-3.7 thinking mode showed no gain over non-thinking.
limits: Tasks have simulation checks, so they are more well-structured than real design.
agent_relevance: Shows the gap between a stated design spec and open design. Single-pass is weak, so an S6 loop is needed.

source: Guo et al. (2025) EngDesign, iterative design with simulator feedback
finding: Feeding the previous design plus score, metrics and logs back for another try raised success steadily. Where the model lacked domain skill, iteration did not help.
numbers: o3 reaches almost 60% pass rate after ten iterations (versus 34.38% single shot). Analog IC design stayed at 0% after ten iterations.
quote: model performance consistently improves with additional iterations
limits: Gain depends on a real evaluator. 'Almost 60%' is the paper's wording; figure values not extracted.
agent_relevance: Evidence for G2 (revise from real output) in design-like search: feedback loops add roughly 25 points but cannot create missing knowledge.

source: Guo et al. (2025) EngDesign, chain-of-thought on open tasks and failure types
finding: Chain-of-thought gave a small average gain for GPT-4o on the open-ended subset, with some domains worse. Failure categories include constraint violation, over-reliance on prior textbook patterns and hallucination.
numbers: GPT-4o on EngDesign-Open, overall: pass rate 14.29% with CoT vs 12.70% without; score 42.89 vs 37.50. Some domains fell with CoT.
limits: Few tasks per domain so noise is large. GPT-4o only.
agent_relevance: A thinking prompt alone moves little in design. The loop and the check matter more (G7).

source: Gu et al. (2025/2026) EngiBench: hierarchical engineering problem solving
finding: Three levels from formula use to open-ended under-specified modelling. Accuracy falls as the problem becomes more ill-structured. Small input rewrites hurt weaker models. Humans beat all models on the open level.
numbers: Level 1 accuracy mostly roughly 77-98% across many models. Gemini 2.5 Flash drops only 1.2% under perturbation. Level 3 (rubric 0-10): GPT-4.1 and Claude 3.7 Sonnet average above 6, Mixtral-8x7B below 4. Llama 4 scores 0 on multi-objective decision-making where GPT-4.1 gets 7.5.
limits: Level 3 is graded by LLMs on a rubric, then calibrated by humans. Exact human score numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: The drop from structured to open-ended levels is the measured version of Simon's well- vs ill-structured split. Weak spots are trade-offs and uncertainty.

source: Egea et al. (2025) ChatGPT as an inventor: LLM vs engineering students in a 48-hour hackathon
finding: ChatGPT-4 directed two human builders to design a Nerf dart launcher. It finished second of six teams. It generated concepts well but dropped a promising concept after a minor setback and fixated on one concept.
numbers: 116 prototypes in total. Distance: winner 37 m, ChatGPT team 14.8 m (2nd, almost 3 m above team mean), others 8.1, 6.6, 5.1, 0.1 m.
quote: Alright, given the challenges with the pneumatic launcher, we might want to pivot to another mechanism
limits: One task, one run, one LLM team. Humans acted as hands, which adds noise. Ranking of 6 teams has no statistics.
agent_relevance: Two search failures to guard against in S6: abandoning a good branch after one failure, and sticking to a single concept. It dropped the pneumatic concept after valves did not fit; the winner kept it.

source: Egea et al. (2025) ChatGPT as an inventor, recommendations and fixation
finding: The model leaned to the common concept types (pneumatic, spring, elastic) and added unneeded complexity. Authors recommend asking it for alternatives and giving it subsystem-sized tasks.
numbers: Six recommendations: use for ideation, keep human oversight on key decisions, iterative feedback loops, prompt for alternatives, subsystem-level tasks, ask it to avoid fixation.
limits: Observational. Recommendations are not tested.
agent_relevance: A forced-alternatives step triggered by a failed test (not by schedule, G1) addresses the premature pivot problem.

source: Ma, Grandi, McComb, Goucher-Lambert (2024) Exploring the Capabilities of LLMs for Generating Diverse Design Solutions
finding: GPT-4 produced less diverse design solutions than crowd humans under every setting tried. Sampling parameters had no clean monotonic effect. Prompt wording changed diversity.
numbers: 4,000 LLM solutions; 5 design topics; 8 temperature/top-p combinations; 8 prompt methods; 4 diversity metrics; 100 human crowd solutions per topic. Best parameter pair temperature 1, top-p 1 (the default).
limits: GPT-4 only. Diversity is embedding-based, not expert judgment. The max-temperature plus max-top-p pair was incoherent and excluded.
agent_relevance: The breadth of the generate step is a limit in design search. Wider sampling alone does not close the gap to people.

source: Ma et al. (2024) diversity study, prompt technique results
finding: A second pass in which the model critiques and edits its own 50 solutions gave the largest diversity gain. A persona asking for far-fetched ideas also helped. The word 'unique' scored lower than 'creative' or 'novel'.
numbers: Critique-critique was the best method; no prompt method reached human diversity. Logistic regression on embeddings separated LLM from human solutions in some topics (milk frother most) but not others.
limits: Effects shown in heatmaps, not significance tests. Authors call the semantic-gap result inconclusive.
agent_relevance: A critique-and-edit pass widens the option set. Use it on a signal, with code measuring diversity (G1, G8).

source: Shin, Polyanskaya, Lucero, Oulasvirta (2025) No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing (CHI)
finding: Experiment with 280 designers. GPT-4o help (direct frames, free chat, or a structured Dorst nine-step process) did not raise novelty or usefulness of problem frames over working alone.
numbers: N = 280 designers, 4 conditions (manual, direct, structured, free-form), 3 design problems, 15 expert raters. Mean time for two frames: manual 23.25 min, direct 21.82, structured 28.35, free-form 20.78. No significant quality difference. LLMs widened the gap: more competent designers made more novel frames.
quote: using LLMs does not help improve the quality of problem frames
limits: Crowd platform participants. GPT-4o in August 2024, one model. Human users, not an autonomous loop.
agent_relevance: Strong boundary: reframing the problem is the hardest design step and a plain LLM did not help humans do it. Any reframing operator must be tested, not assumed.

source: Shin et al. (2025) problem reframing study, behaviour in LLM conditions
finding: In the structured Dorst-based condition nearly everyone regenerated all LLM content at least once. Direct-frame users also kept regenerating. Inexperienced users reported lower agency. Authors link this to fixation on high-fidelity LLM text.
numbers: Structured condition: all but one participant regenerated all content at least once; 'apparent problem' regenerated 39 times, 'stakeholders perspective' 25 times.
limits: Counts are descriptive.
agent_relevance: Fluent model output can anchor. Keep frames as short candidates scored by code, not accepted prose.

source: Wray, Kirk, Laird (2024) Eliciting Problem Specifications via Large Language Models
finding: An LLM agent workflow turns a natural-language task into a Newell-style problem space (states, operators, goal) that Soar can search with weak methods. The LLM does the problem-formulation step that Simon found hard to automate.
numbers: Feasibility test on water-jug problems (GPT-4-0125-preview, temperature 0), three settings: CoT solve, CoT formulation, multi-node CTA agent. CoT solved easy cases and sometimes F(9,17)->5 in 20 steps. In the mixed-units variant (4 qt, 9 gal) the CTA agent handled units; CoT formulation never did. The test-case node was weakest.
limits: One problem family; preliminary; larger model needed for precise specs; no success rates reported.
agent_relevance: A template for S1-S6: have the model write the problem space (states, operators, goal test) first, then let code search it.

source: Wray, Kirk, Laird (2024) problem-space paper, relation to Soar and interactive task learning
finding: Positions the work against Soar interactive task learning, where a human gives goals, constraints and actions. The aim is to remove the human translator so a cognitive system can attack problems nobody has formalised.
numbers: Weak methods named as still critical in current agents: hill climbing, breadth-first, depth-first, means-ends analysis.
limits: Conceptual argument. Kirk et al. 2024 (LLM plus ITL) not read.
agent_relevance: Weak methods are cheap, code-run search. The model only supplies the formal problem space.

source: Song (2025) Where to Search: Measure the Prior-Structured Search Space of LLM Agents
finding: Formal theory of generate-filter-refine loops: an agent as a fuzzy relation over inputs and outputs, paths weighted by a continuation parameter, giving a reachability-difficulty measure. Says search quality depends on how the domain prior shapes the hypothesis space.
numbers: Theory paper; validated with two instantiations (details not recorded).
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read closely. Formalism untested outside the author's cases.
agent_relevance: A way to measure how far a set of operators can reach.

source: Kim et al. (2025) GraphicBench and GraphicTown: planning for graphic design with language agents
finding: Open-ended creative design planning by an LLM agent with 46 tools. Plans looked right but often did not produce successful outcomes when executed.
numbers: 1,079 queries, 4 design types, 6 LLMs. Main error classes: spatial reasoning between components, global dependencies across experts, invalid action retrieval. VQA pass rate across models roughly 27.5 to 39.6.
limits: Outcomes judged by automatic proxies (CLIPScore, template match, VQA, model-rated creativity).
agent_relevance: A plan that looks sound is not a pass (G3). Execute and test.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) LLM-Modulo, plain-prompt planning table
finding: Plain LLM planning stays near the floor in an obfuscated domain whatever the model, which suggests it relies on recognising the familiar domain.
numbers: Mystery Blocksworld, 600 instances per model: most models solved under 3%; the same models solved much more on plain Blocksworld.
limits: Table text garbled in extraction, so only the pattern is reported.
agent_relevance: Test the scaffold on re-labelled problems to check it searches rather than recalls.

source: Newell and Simon (1972) Human Problem Solving; Newell and Simon (1976) heuristic search hypothesis
finding: Foundational claim: a physical symbol system solves problems by generating and modifying symbol structures until a solution appears. The problem space of states and operators is the unit of analysis.
numbers: Lab protocols: cryptarithmetic, logic, chess; GPS built from think-aloud transcripts. Cited from memory and from secondary text in Wray et al. and Yao et al.
limits: Tasks were well-structured. Critics say the model misses framing and context.
agent_relevance: Gives the vocabulary for states, operators, goal test and search control.

source: Simon (1973) The structure of ill-structured problems; Simon (1969/1996) The Sciences of the Artificial
finding: Simon argued ill-structured problems are handled by the same machinery: the solver draws on memory and constraints and builds a well-structured sub-problem to search. Design is satisficing search, not optimising.
numbers: No experiment; theoretical argument. Not opened; from memory.
limits: Contested by Schon (reflection in action) and by situated approaches.
agent_relevance: Supports: fix a working frame, search inside it, reframe only on impasse (G1).

source: Goel and Pirolli (1992) The structure of design problem spaces; Dorst and Cross (2001) co-evolution of problem and solution
finding: Design protocols show problem structuring, phase transitions and problem and solution spaces developing together. Pure forward search is not the whole story.
numbers: Protocol analyses of small numbers of designers. Not opened; Dorst and Cross cited inside Shin et al.
limits: Small samples, think-aloud, few tasks.
agent_relevance: Motivates a reframe operator coupled to search state. Shin et al. show LLMs do not reliably help humans do this.

source: Older AI search systems: GPS, Soar, R1/XCON, AM, BACON
finding: GPS used means-ends analysis. Soar treats every decision as search in problem spaces and learns chunks at impasses. R1 configured computers with rule-based search.
numbers: No numbers recorded this session.
limits: These systems needed a human-written problem space. Wray et al. 2024 test LLMs for that step.
agent_relevance: Impasse then subgoal is the same trigger as our impasse detector (G1).

source: Kirk et al. (2024) LLM-integrated interactive task learning in Soar, as cited by Wray et al.
finding: A Soar agent extracts task knowledge from an LLM, reducing human feedback while keeping solution quality. Not opened.
numbers: None recorded.
limits: Second-hand through Wray et al.
agent_relevance: Hybrid pattern: symbolic search with an LLM as knowledge source.
